corrected_summary: The May 15, 1846 Council Springs treaty (9 Stat. 844, proclaimed Mar. 8, 1847) was signed by 24 named Comanche men (among them Buffalo Hump, Old Owl and Santa Anna, leaders historians identify as Penateka) and by Waco, Keechi, Tonkawa, Wichita and Tawakoni signers. The treaty text names no bands, so 'only one band' rests on historians' identification of the signers. It acknowledges US protection and trade regulation; it cedes no land.

The 1835 treaty (7 Stat. 474) was made with the Comanche, Wichita and eastern tribes and does not name the Kiowa. source_title: Treaty with the Kioway, Ka-ta-ka and Ta-wa-ka-ro, Fort Gibson, May 26, 1837

corrected_summary: Ten Kiowa signed the May 26, 1837 treaty (7 Stat. 533), including Ta-ka-ta-couche, Sen-son-da-cat and Ka-him-hi, as the book says, and also To-ho-sa, 'Top of the Mountain', whom Mooney identifies as Dohasan ('Little Bluff'). The claim that Dohasan never signed is contradicted. Article 4 gave all parties free permission to hunt and trap on the Great Prairie west of the Cross Timbers; Article 8 gave presents after signing. Three Kiowa Apache (as Ka-ta-ka) also signed. No land was ceded.
notes: Mooney line: To-ho-sa, "Top of the Mountain" (Doha-san, "Little Bluff"). The identification is Mooney's.

source_title: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa and Apache, Fort Atkinson, July 27, 1853 (with 1854 amendments)
source_quote: TO-HAU-SEN, his x mark (Little Mountain) chief Kiowas
corrected_summary: The 1853 treaty lists To-hau-sen (Little Mountain), whom Mooney identifies as Dohasan, as 'chief Kiowas', first among six Kiowa signers; Si-tank-ki (Sitting Bear, Setangya) signed as 'war chief'. Both also signed the July 21, 1854 acceptance of the Senate amendments. The claim that Setangya signed for the tribe while Dohasan withheld assent is contradicted by the treaty text. Continued raiding is documented (Mooney), but 'lacked broad consent' is an inference.
corrected_instrument_cite: 10 Stat. 1013 (concluded July 27, 1853; Senate amendments Apr. 12, 1854; accepted July 21, 1854; proclaimed Feb. 12, 1855, misprinted 1854 in the Statutes)
notes: Mooney index: 'LITTLE-MOUNTAIN, see DOHASAN'. Kappler page 600 not re-checked.

source_title: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa and Apache, Fort Atkinson, July 27, 1853 (with 1854 amendments)
source_quote: out roads or highways
corrected_summary: Article 3 recognizes the US right to lay off roads or highways, make 'reservations of land necessary thereto', locate depots and establish military and other posts in the tribes' territories. The text sets no width. The claim that the nations understood a road no wider than a wagon track, and the 'two miles wide' figure, are the author's and cite no source.
notes: Article 3 is a right-of-way and posts concession, not a cession. Treat the 'wagon-wheel' understanding as the author's assertion.

source_title: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa and Apache, Fort Atkinson, July 27, 1853 (with 1854 amendments)

notes: Art. 4 refers to persons 'passing through their said territories'; Art. 6 compensates losses from 'travel of the people of the United States through their territories'. The treaty has no cession article. The 1854 acceptance of the Senate amendments was signed by Comanche and Kiowa only; no Apache signed it.

corrected_summary: Chivington's Colorado volunteers attacked the Cheyenne and Arapaho camp at Sand Creek on Nov. 29, 1864, under a US flag. Death counts vary by source (Mooney gives 120; other estimates run from about 150 to 200 or more, mostly women, children and elders). Mooney notes that recollection of the massacre made bringing the Kiowa and Comanche to the 1865 council difficult.

corrected_summary: On Nov. 25, 1864, Carson's New Mexico volunteers and Ute and Jicarilla scouts burned a Kiowa village of 176 tipis on the Canadian near Adobe Walls, destroying most of its winter provisions and hides; the Kiowa saved their horses and Carson withdrew. Kiowa accounts give five dead. Carson was a US commissioner at the Little Arkansas in October 1865 (14 Stat. 717).

source_title: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas, Oct. 18, 1865

corrected_instrument_cite: 14 Stat. 717 (concluded Oct. 18, 1865; ratified May 22, 1866; proclaimed May 26, 1866); Kappler II 892
notes: Preamble calls signers 'duly authorized'. Comanche signers are listed for the Yamparika, Penateka, Nokoni, Kotsoteka and Tenawa bands; no Kwahadi signer appears. Royce 510 belongs to 1867, not 1865. Kappler page not re-checked.

source_title: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas, Oct. 18, 1865
source_quote: shall be and is hereby set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the tribes who are parties to this treaty
corrected_summary: Article II boundaries are as stated, but the grant covered the described district 'or such portion of the same as may hereafter from time to time be designated by the President', so 'absolute' was qualified. The ICC (26 Ind. Cl. Comm. 101, 102) describes the tract as about 39,630,000 acres in northwestern Texas and western Oklahoma (Royce 510 and 511); it does not include Colorado or Kansas. Medicine Lodge (1867) reduced it to Royce 510.
notes: Do not draw the 1865 reserve in Colorado. The Colorado and Kansas lands are Royce 478 (relinquished). ICC acreage at library/icc/d257_v26_p101.txt.

source_title: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas, Oct. 18, 1865
source_quote: more especially their claims and rights in and to the country north of the Cimarone river and west of the eastern boundary of New Mexico
notes: Relinquishment of all claims outside the reserve, especially north of the Cimarron. Art. VI confirms bands were absent. The Senate resolution of May 22, 1866 names only the 'chiefs and headmen of the Kiowa tribe'. Art. III let the tribes keep ranging south of the Arkansas until removal, so the relinquishment did not end use of SE Colorado south of the Arkansas in 1865.

source_title: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas, Oct. 18, 1865
source_quote: expressly permitted to reside upon and range at pleasure throughout the unsettled portions of that part of the country they claim as originally theirs, which lies south of the Arkansas river
notes: Limited to 'unsettled portions' and to the period before removal. Medicine Lodge Art. 16 repeats the hunting right on 'the lands south of the Arkansas river, formerly called theirs'. 'US admission of their original claim' is the K1 pass's reading.

corrected_summary: The Kiowa and Comanche did not agree to settle in western Kansas: their 1865 reserve lay south of the Kansas line in present Oklahoma and Texas. The Kansas exclusion was a Senate amendment to the Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty of Oct. 14, 1865 (14 Stat. 703), requiring that no part of their reservation be within Kansas. Mooney confirms Dohasan protested and the treaty was signed anyway; he signed as To-hau-son (Little Mountain), with Satanta, Satank, Lone Wolf and Kicking Eagle.
corrected_instrument_cite: 14 Stat. 717; 14 Stat. 703 (Senate amendment to Art. II)

notes: Art. IV compensation was to be what 'the Congress of the United States, may be deemed just and proper', so discretionary. Art. V: $10 per capita until removal, $15 after, for forty years. Medicine Lodge Art. X substituted new annuities 'in lieu of' those under the 1865 treaty. The author's 'little or no evidence' of compensation was not re-checked (appropriation acts 14-15 Stat.).

source_title: Act of Mar. 29, 1867, ch. 13, sec. 6; Act of July 20, 1867, ch. 34; Taylor report as quoted in ICC Docket 257 dissent
source_cite: 15 Stat. 9; 15 Stat. 18; 15 Stat. 17; 26 Ind. Cl. Comm. 101 (Kuykendall dissent, c. p.123ff)
source_quote: large territory be set apart south of the southern line of Kansas and west of Arkansas, including the present
corrected_summary: The facts are confirmed: sec. 6 of the Act of Mar. 29, 1867 (15 Stat. 9) repealed the laws allowing executive officers to make Indian treaties, and Commissioner Taylor's report (quoted in the Docket 257 dissent) asked that this repeal be undone and recommended a large territory south of Kansas, including the Texas staked plains, as the home for all Indians south of the Platte. Congress did undo the repeal on July 20, 1867 (15 Stat. 18, ch. 34), the same day it created the Peace Commission (15 Stat. 17), whose sec. 2 directed it to select districts for permanent homes. That the commission was 'designed for removal, not negotiation' is the author's reading.
corrected_instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 7, 9 (ch. 13, sec. 6); repealed by 15 Stat. 18 (ch. 34); Peace Commission Act 15 Stat. 17 (ch. 32)

source_quote: commencing at a point where the Washita river crosses the 98th meridian
corrected_summary: The Medicine Lodge reservation lay between the Washita (north) and the Red and North Fork of the Red (south and west), east to the 98th meridian, not between the Canadian and the Red. Article XI bound the tribes to withdraw opposition to railroads and military posts. 'Forcibly coerced by threats of starvation and military intimidation' is the Kansapedia characterization; the treaty text and Mooney do not establish threats, though the setting (a large military escort and ration supply) is documented elsewhere.

Whether he was the only Kiowa leader who did not sign cannot be shown from the signer list. Kicking Bird (Ton-a-en-ko) and Satanta did sign.

source_quote: are put in brackets with an asterisk are written in the original with black pencil, the rest of the original treaty being written with black ink.
corrected_summary: In Article II only two items are bracketed as pencil: the word 'the' before 'following district' and the phrase 'with the consent of the United States'. The boundary description itself is in ink. Other pencil additions are in Article XI: the word 'river', the clause barring white settlement for three years on the old Cheyenne, Arapaho and Apache reservation of Oct. 14, 1865, and 'the said tribes'. The claim that leaders rejected the boundaries and that they were inserted into a pre-drafted document is the author's interpretation and needs the council proceedings.
notes: The pencil phrase 'with the consent of the United States' limiting whom the tribes could admit is correctly identified.

source_title: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge, Oct. 21, 1867
source_quote: any lands south of the Arkansas [river, *] so long as the buffalo may
corrected_summary: Article XI reserved the right to hunt on 'any lands south of the Arkansas' so long as the buffalo ranged there in numbers to justify the chase. That area includes SE Colorado south of the Arkansas, not only Kansas or Kansas and Texas. Henderson's remark and the recorded laughter come from the council transcript and were not checked.
notes: Needs the Peace Commission proceedings for the Henderson quote.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (17th Annual Report BAE, 1898)
source_quote: General Sherman, in September, asked to have all issues whatever to any of these tribes withheld until they had concentrated near Fort Cobb
corrected_summary: The Senate did not advise ratification until July 25, 1868 (proclaimed Aug. 25, 1868), so treaty provisions were not yet in force in early 1868. In September 1868 Sherman asked that all issues be withheld until the tribes concentrated near Fort Cobb. The claim that none of the promised rations had been delivered by 1871 was not verified (ARCIA 1869-1871 would settle it).

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (17th Annual Report BAE, 1898)
source_cite: Mooney 1898, Further insolence (p.188-189), Release of Set-t'ainte (p.195), Set-t'ainte (p.206-207)
source_quote: he committed suicide by throwing himself from an upper story of the prison, October 11, 1878
corrected_summary: In 1871 Sherman had Satanta, Satank (Setangya) and Big Tree arrested; Satank resisted and was killed on the way; Satanta and Big Tree were tried in Texas, the death sentence was commuted, and they were released Oct. 8, 1873. Satanta was re-arrested in fall 1874, returned to Huntsville prison in November 1874, and died by suicide Oct. 11, 1878. Forced railroad labor is not in Mooney and is unverified.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (17th Annual Report BAE, 1898)
source_cite: Mooney 1898, Further insolence (p.189, agent's 1872 report); calendar summer 1879 (p.344)
source_quote: By withholding rations for three months, he had compelled them to bring in two captives without ransom
corrected_summary: The agent (Tatum, 1869-1873) withheld rations to force the return of captives, per his 1872 report as summarized by Mooney, not as documented for cultural change. In 1879 the Kiowa killed and ate their ponies after the buffalo hunt failed, and the agent's report speaks of 'insufficient rations'; that agent presented the hunger as a push toward farming. 'Lowered rations to starvation levels to press assimilation' overstates what these sources show.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (17th Annual Report BAE, 1898)
source_cite: Mooney 1898, Progress of the campaign (p.210-211) and Surrender of the Comanche (p.214)
source_quote: destroying over a hundred tipis and capturing their entire camp outfit, with over fourteen hundred horses and mules
corrected_summary: On Sept. 26-27, 1874 Mackenzie surprised a camp of Cheyenne and allies in a canyon near Red River (Palo Duro), destroyed over a hundred tipis and captured over 1,400 horses and mules (many later shot). The Kiowa came in mostly by February 1875, but Quanah's Kwahadi Comanche did not surrender until June 2, 1875, so not all had surrendered by April 1875.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (17th Annual Report BAE, 1898)
source_cite: Mooney 1898, Leasing of grass lands (p.219-220); Measles epidemic of 1892 (p.223)
source_quote: the Kiowa and Apache for a year longer refused to accept the money
corrected_summary: Grass leasing began informally; the first payment (summer 1885) went to the Comanche, while the Kiowa and Apache refused the money for one more year, fearing a scheme to take their land. They later took grass money, and in 1892 Lone Wolf was among the delegates who negotiated leases of nearly all surplus grass lands. 'Continually refused to lease' is contradicted. No act of Congress barring Kiowa from leaving the reservation after an 1879 killing was found; that claim is unsupported as stated.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (17th Annual Report BAE, 1898)
source_cite: Mooney 1898, Death of Sun-boy, Ghost dance (p.221-222), Measles epidemic of 1892 (p.223), agents list (p.225)
source_quote: resulting in the death of about two hundred and twenty persons, nearly all children, among the Kiowa and Apache
corrected_summary: In January 1891 three boys ran away from the agency school 'in consequence of the harshness of a teacher' and froze to death. The 1892 measles epidemic, spread when the superintendent sent sick children home, killed about 220 people, nearly all children, among the Kiowa and Apache. The last Kiowa sun dance was attempted in 1890 and stopped by troops on the agent's order; E. E. White was special agent 1887-1888, but an 1888 ban by him was not verified. 'Beaten' and 'captured' were not verified.

source_title: Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock
source_cite: 187 U.S. 553 (statement of the case, bill's allegations); Mooney 1898, Commission for allotment (p.224)
source_quote: fraudulent misrepresentations of its terms by the interpreters
corrected_summary: The general claim is the author's. For the 1892 Jerome agreement, the Kiowa complaint in Lone Wolf alleged signatures were obtained by interpreters' misrepresentation, and Mooney reports that the Indians denounced the interpreter and asked to have their names struck. These are allegations recorded by the sources, not findings of fact.

The three-year bar on white settlement applied to the old reservation of the Cheyenne, Arapaho and Apache treaty of Oct. 14, 1865, not to the 1865 Kiowa-Comanche reservation, and the clause is a pencil addition. The 'hollow promise' because the military was killing buffalo is PSL's interpretation; no primary source was checked.

VI let a head of family who wished to begin farming select up to 320 acres (and any other person over 18 up to 80 acres) within the reservation; it was an optional farming selection, not a division of the land. source_cite: ICC Docket 32: 5 Ind. Cl. Comm. 72, 96 (Mar. 12, 1957); 5 Ind. Cl. Comm. 297 (July 18, 1957)
source_quote: Additional findings - Offsets
corrected_summary: In Docket 32 the ICC made offset findings on Mar. 12, 1957 and reconsidered offsets in an amended final order of July 18, 1957 (5 Ind. Cl. Comm. 297). The award was $2,067,166, affirmed by the Court of Claims in 1958; certiorari was denied in 1959. Kansapedia's 'nearly $2 million in 1960' is off on the date. The 1900 Act itself (31 Stat. 680) barred applying the agreement money to Indian depredation judgments. The $1.5 million depredation figure was not verified.

source_title: ICC Docket 32 opinion (Apr. 9, 1951) and additional findings (Dec. 13, 1955)
source_cite: 1 Ind. Cl. Comm. 505, 528 (1951); 4 Ind. Cl. Comm. 95 (1955), finding 22; 5 Ind. Cl. Comm. 297 (July 18, 1957)
source_quote: acquired the land without the consent of the Indians upon
corrected_summary: The ICC did not find the land 'unconscionably' acquired in 1951. It held that Congress so changed the Jerome Agreement that 'the Government acquired the land without the consent of the Indians upon its own terms', and said it was 'not necessary to determine' whether the agreement was obtained by fraud, duress or an unconscionable consideration, or whether three fourths signed (1 Ind. Cl. Comm. 505, 528). Additional findings of Dec. 13, 1955 set the ceded area at 2,033,583 acres worth $4,067,166 ($2.00 an acre) as of June 6, 1900 (4 Ind. Cl. Comm. 95). The amended final order was July 18, 1957 (not Mar. 29, 1957); award $2,067,166; affirmed by the Court of Claims July 16, 1958; certiorari denied Mar. 9, 1959.
corrected_instrument_cite: ICC Docket 32, 1 Ind. Cl. Comm. 505 (1951), 4 Ind. Cl. Comm. 95 (1955), 5 Ind. Cl. Comm. 297 (1957), aff'd 143 Ct. Cl. 534 (1958)
notes: The acreage and value are confirmed (library/icc/d032_v04_p095.txt, finding 22). The 'without consent' holding is the strongest ICC language and should be the map's wording, not 'unconscionable'.

source_title: Indian Claims Commission Act, Aug. 13, 1946
source_quote: either party may appeal from the determination
corrected_summary: Section 22 does make payment a full discharge and bars further claims, as quoted. But section 20(b) gave 'either party' the right to appeal an ICC determination to the Court of Claims, so the tribes' appeal rights were not barred; in Docket 32 the tribes cross-appealed in 1958. The claim of a one-sided appeal right is contradicted.

source_title: ICC Docket 257 opinion (1971) and Findings on compromise settlement (1974)
source_quote: 39,630,000 acres located in the northwestern part of the present State of Texas and the western portion of the present State of Oklahoma
corrected_summary: The ICC described the 1865 recognized-title tract as about 39,630,000 acres in northwestern Texas and western Oklahoma (Royce 510 and 511), not in Kansas or Colorado; the book altered the location and acreage. SE Colorado appeared only in the tribes' alternative aboriginal-title claim (about 100 million acres, Royce 478, 510, 511), which was never adjudicated. The Aug. 9, 1971 summary judgment of recognized title was reversed by the Court of Claims on June 20, 1973 (202 Ct. Cl. 29); certiorari was denied Apr. 15, 1974. The $35,060,000 ($35,000,000 in Docket 257 and $60,000 in Docket 259-A) was a compromise settlement approved July 17, 1974 (34 Ind. Cl. Comm. 263), with waiver of appeal, settling all claims that were or could have been asserted. 'Largest ICC award ever' was not verified.
corrected_instrument_cite: ICC Dockets 257 and 259-A, 34 Ind. Cl. Comm. 263 (1974) (compromise); summary judgment at 26 Ind. Cl. Comm. 101 rev'd 202 Ct. Cl. 29 (1973)
corrected_royce_areas: 511 (1865 reserve, ceded 1867 except 510); 478 for SE Colorado
notes: The map must not say the ICC found recognized title in Colorado. The Colorado aboriginal claim was released by the 1974 compromise without any finding. The settlement findings note Ernest Wallace's report placing the 1865 range into Colorado along the Purgatoire, and that the ICC had found part of SE Colorado aboriginally Jicarilla (Docket 22-A).

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (book text)
source_quote: the settlement was negligible when juxtaposed against the value of other land in the area being sold for $11.00 per acre
corrected_summary: These are PSL's arguments. Arithmetic: $35,060,000 over about 39,630,000 acres (the ICC's figure) is about $0.88 per acre, and it was a compromise, not a valuation; Docket 32 valued the 1900 cession at $2.00 per acre. The book gives the buffalo loss as $48 billion here and $46 billion on p.92. The 1834 Act's $1,000 penalty (sec. 11) applied to settling on lands 'belonging, secured, or granted by treaty'. The $11 per acre comparison and the $12 billion interest figure were not verified.

source_title: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa and Apache, Fort Atkinson, July 27, 1853 (with 1854 amendments)
source_quote: SI-TAH-LE, his x mark (Poor Wolf) chief Apache
notes: Apache signers in 1853: Si-tah-le (Poor Wolf), Oh-ah-te-kah (Poor Bear), Ah-zaah (Prairie Wolf), Kootz-zah (The Cigar). The $18,000 a year was for all three tribes together, divided by population. No Apache signed the July 21, 1854 acceptance of the Senate amendments.

source_title: Treaty with the Kiowa, Comanche and Apache (Apache adhesion), Medicine Lodge, Oct. 21, 1867
source_quote: shall be shared equally by the Apaches
corrected_summary: The 1867 Apache adhesion confederated the Apache with the Kiowa and Comanche on an equal footing and gave them an equal share of annuities and benefits. It did not acknowledge territorial claims; in Art. IV the Apache relinquished all rights under the 1865 Cheyenne and Arapaho treaties. Historical ties to the Front Range and SE Colorado are PSL's statement; Mooney identifies the 'Kaskaia' at an 1815 South Platte gathering as probably the Kiowa Apache.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (17th Annual Report BAE, 1898)
source_quote: five persons of the allied tribes, including two women, were killed
corrected_summary: Carson attacked the Kiowa winter camp near Adobe Walls on Nov. 25, 1864. Kiowa accounts recorded by Mooney give five dead in all, including a young Apache warrior and an old Apache man; 'heavy losses' for the Apache is not supported. The Apache did leave the Kiowa-Comanche confederation for the Cheyenne and Arapaho by the treaty of Oct. 17, 1865 (14 Stat. 713). The motive ascribed is PSL's reading, though Pettis says the aim was to disable the tribes in winter camp.

source_title: Treaty with the Apache, Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 17, 1865
source_quote: advise and consent to the ratification of the treaty between the United States, by their Commissioners, and the chiefs and headmen of the Apaches and Cheyennes and Ar[r]apahoes
corrected_summary: The Oct. 17, 1865 Apache treaty was ratified May 22, 1866 and proclaimed May 26, 1866 (14 Stat. 713). The Oct. 14, 1865 Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty was ratified with amendments (including that no part of the reservation be in Kansas); Apache chiefs assented at Fort Zarah on Nov. 19, 1866, and it was proclaimed Feb. 2, 1867 (14 Stat. 703). It is not true that the treaties were never ratified; the promised reservation was never established. The Apache signers are as listed. The 320-acre and 160-acre grants were to Sand Creek chiefs and to widows and orphans of Sand Creek. The $39,050 appropriation and the 'returned to Treasury' account were not verified.

source_title: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 14, 1865 (Apache joined Oct. 17)
source_quote: as originally theirs, which lies between the Arkansas and Platte rivers
corrected_summary: Under the Oct. 14, 1865 treaty, which the Apache joined on Oct. 17, the tribes could range, until removal, over the unsettled country they claimed as originally theirs between the Arkansas and the Platte, which lies north of the Arkansas and includes eastern Colorado. PSL's location of the Apache in the Arkansas valley between SE Colorado and Kansas in 1865-1867 is an inference.

source_title: Treaty with the Kiowa, Comanche and Apache (Apache adhesion), Medicine Lodge, Oct. 21, 1867
source_quote: Phi li p Mc Cusk er , Interpreter.
corrected_summary: The Apache adhesion's attestation lists only Philip McCusker (the Comanche interpreter) as interpreter, which is consistent with PSL's point that the Apache had no interpreter of their own on the record. The relay through Arapaho, the seven languages and Sherman's 50,000 rations come from secondary accounts and the council proceedings, not checked.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (17th Annual Report BAE, 1898)
corrected_summary: Mooney's table gives the Apache population as 325 in 1891, confirming that figure. 'Unwilling loss, under duress' is PSL's characterization. The statement that the tribes never received any of the promised annuities is overstated: Mooney records regular annuity issues at the agency (e.g. 1892), though shortfalls and withholding are documented.

source_title: Act of June 6, 1900 (ratifying the Oct. 6/21, 1892 agreement)
source_quote: of two million (2,000,000) dollars, as follows: Five hundred thousand
corrected_summary: The 1892 agreement as ratified gave 160 acres to each member (adults and children), set aside 480,000 acres of common grazing land, and paid $2,000,000 for the rest, with 5 percent interest on unpaid sums. The ICC later found the ceded area to be 2,033,583 acres. Mooney reports 1892 grass leases of 'nearly $100,000' a year, about equal to 5 percent of $2 million; the $210,000 biannual figure was not verified. The point that 160 acres could not sustain farming or ranching is PSL's.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (book text)
source_quote: It is recommended that the State of Colorado support the Kiowa, Comanche, and Apache Tribes of Oklahoma Nation in its efforts to have the Indian Claims Commis- sion settlement opened for appeal.
notes: These are PSL policy recommendations, not historical findings.

source_title: Trade and Intercourse Act, June 30, 1834
source_quote: States west of the Mississippi, and not within the states of Missouri and
corrected_summary: The 1834 Act defined Indian country as US land west of the Mississippi outside Missouri, Louisiana and Arkansas Territory, and section 11 fined settlement on lands 'belonging, secured, or granted by treaty'. But in 1834 the country south of the Arkansas in present Colorado was Mexican territory, so the Act did not reach it until after 1848. The failure-to-correct claim is PSL's interpretation.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (17th Annual Report BAE, 1898)
source_cite: Mooney 1898, Indian war on the plains, 1864 (p.176-177)
source_quote: whom all persons were authorized to kill and destroy as enemies of the country
corrected_summary: Mooney confirms that Governor Evans's summer 1864 proclamation authorized citizens to kill Indians remaining out as hostiles. 'Genocide' and state liability are PSL's characterizations. The Kiowa and Comanche relinquishment of SE Colorado was by the 1865 and 1867 federal treaties, not an Evans removal.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (book text)
source_quote: The School Fund received 4 million acres of land in Colorado to support schools
notes: Colorado's school grant was sections 16 and 36 under the Enabling Act of Mar. 3, 1875 (18 Stat. 474); total acreage not checked (Colorado State Land Board records would settle it).

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (book text)
source_quote: According to the US Forest Service there are over 200 sacred sites that are not currently protected.
notes: Needs GOCO rules and a USFS source; neither checked.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (book text)
source_quote: There were approximately five million buffalo in the southern herd.
notes: Hornaday, The Extermination of the American Bison (1889), would settle the herd estimate. The book's value is $46 billion here and $48 billion on p.74; the figure is PSL's calculation.

source_title: Indian Citizenship Act, June 2, 1924
source_quote: impair or otherwise affect the right of any Indian to tribal or other property
corrected_summary: The 1924 Act has no 'protectorate clause'. Its only proviso says citizenship does not impair Indians' rights to tribal or other property. Nothing in it exempts tribal members living off-reservation in Colorado from state property tax. The reserved-right argument is PSL's legal position, not a statutory provision.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 report (book text)
source_quote: The Kiowa eventually avoided termination by refusing to cooperate with the federal government.
notes: Needs Collier's 1934 Anadarko meeting records and the Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act, June 26, 1936 (49 Stat. 1967). The IRA's allotment ban (48 Stat. 984, sec. 1) was not extended to Oklahoma until OIWA; not checked.
